title: A grid in memory
sub: T[,], jagged and flat arrays, neighbors by offsets, Island Perimeter and Game of Life in place
cards/0/title: Three ways to store a tile map
cards/0/body:
A w×h tile map — walkability, tile type, step cost. In C# you can store it in three ways.

T[,] — a rectangular array. One object, one contiguous block, row-major order: [y, x] and [y, x + 1] sit next to each other. Indexing is convenient, but every access checks bounds in both dimensions, and the sizes come from GetLength(0) (rows) and GetLength(1) (columns) — easy to mix up.

T[][] — a jagged array. An array of references to h separate row arrays: h + 1 objects on the heap, rows wherever the allocator put them, an extra pointer hop on every access. In exchange you can take a whole row: grid[y] is a plain T[]. This is how LeetCode passes grids.

A flat T[] of length w * h, cell (x, y) at index y * w + x. One block, one bounds check, easy to hand to Span<T>, NativeArray<T>, Jobs and Burst. The price is doing the index math by hand.

Locality. The CPU reads memory in cache lines — usually 64 bytes, i.e. 16 ints. Walking memory sequentially costs one miss per 16 cells; jumping down a column of a 1024-wide grid misses on almost every cell. So the outer loop goes over y and the inner one over x.
cards/1/q: A 1024×1024 grid of int is stored flat: cells[y * w + x]. Which traversal is faster, and why?
cards/1/options/0: Outer over y, inner over x — it walks memory in order, one cache miss per 16 cells
cards/1/options/1: Outer over x, inner over y — also in order: the index keeps growing anyway
cards/1/options/2: No difference: array access is O(1) in any order
cards/1/explain: Neighboring x are neighboring memory cells, and one 64-byte cache line brings in 16 cells. An inner loop over y jumps by w · 4 = 4096 bytes — every step lands in a new cache line.
cards/1/wrong/1: The index grows, but in steps of w = 1024 elements, i.e. 4 KB: every access is a new cache line.
cards/1/wrong/2: O(1) counts operations, not time: a cache miss costs tens of times more than a hit. Same asymptotics, different speed.
cards/2/body:
Four ifs for “up, down, left, right” get copied from problem to problem and break differently in each one. Instead use an array of offsets: one loop over directions and one bounds check.

The “inside the grid” test in one comparison: (uint)nx < (uint)w. A negative nx cast to uint becomes a huge number and fails too — two checks for the price of one.

Eight neighbors (with diagonals) — the same arrays with 8 entries. In Unity the same thing is written as an array of Vector2Int or Vector3Int — for Tilemap.GetTile.
cards/3/body:
Island Perimeter (LeetCode #463). A grid of 0 (water) and 1 (land), up to 100×100; there is exactly one island and no lakes inside it. Find the length of its coastline.

Brute force: for every land cell count the sides that face water or the edge: 4 neighbors per cell, O(wh). That is already optimal in time, but there is a shorter formula.

Via adjacencies: every land cell has 4 sides; every pair of adjacent land cells hides two sides — one of each. Perimeter = 4 · land − 2 · adjacencies. To count each pair once, look only right and down.

In a game this is how you measure the border of a region — a fence, a coastline, a selection outline. And “only right and down” is a general trick for not counting a pair twice.
cards/4/q: Compute the island’s perimeter with the formula.
cards/4/wrong/1: 16 − 3: one side per pair was subtracted, but a pair of neighbors hides two — one on each cell.
cards/4/wrong/2: 4 · 4 = 16 — forgot to subtract the sides where land cells touch each other.
cards/5/q: The same count on int[,]. On a 3×5 grid (3 rows, 5 columns) with land in the bottom row the code throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: The check for the neighbor below compares y + 1 with the width w = 5 instead of the height h = 3. On the bottom row y = 2: 3 < 5 passes, and g[3, x] is out of range. On a square grid the bug is invisible — so test on a rectangular one. It should be y + 1 < h.
cards/6/title: Game of Life: two state bits in one cell
cards/6/body:
Game of Life (#289). A cell is live (1) or dead (0). Next generation: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbors (out of 8) survives, otherwise it dies; a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbors comes alive. All cells change simultaneously, the grid is up to 25×25, solve it in place.

The in-place problem: if you write the new state immediately, the neighbors to the right and below will count the new value instead of the old one. Naively — a copy of the grid, O(wh) memory.

Two bits in one cell. A 0 or 1 takes one bit, the other 31 are free. Bit 0 is the current state, bit 1 the next one. The first pass counts neighbors by cell & 1 (the old state; the second bit does not interfere) and, if the cell will live, sets cell |= 2. The second pass shifts: cell >>= 1. Values between the passes: 0 — dead and stays dead, 1 — live, will die, 2 — dead, will come alive, 3 — live and stays live. Bit operations are covered in detail in the bits unit.

In a game a cellular automaton smooths procedural caves (the rule “become a wall if ≥ 5 walls around”). There you usually keep two buffers and swap them — simpler and parallelizable; the bit trick saves memory on huge grids.
cards/7/q: Assemble Game of Life in place.
cards/7/explain: Count a neighbor by its low bit — the old state, even if its “next” bit is already set. A cell will live with three neighbors (any cell) or if it is live with two. Write the future into the second bit, |= 2, leaving the current one alone. The second pass shifts the second bit into the first one’s place. b[y][x] &= 1 would keep the old generation.
cards/8/q: A cell is live and has 4 live neighbors. What value does it hold after the first pass, before the shift?
cards/8/explain: With 4 neighbors a live cell dies: the “next” bit is not set, and the “current” bit stays 1. The value is 0b01 = 1 — “live, will die”. After the shift it becomes 0.
cards/8/wrong/1: 3 = 0b11 means “live and stays live”. But with 4 neighbors a live cell dies.
cards/8/wrong/2: 2 = 0b10 means “dead now, will come alive”. A live cell’s current bit is 1, and the first pass does not change it.
cards/8/wrong/3: The first pass does not touch the current bit — otherwise the neighbors to the right and below would already see it as dead.
cards/9/q: On three live cells in a row in the middle of a 3×3 board the code should produce a vertical triple, but it loses the bottom cell. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/9/explain: After the first pass a surviving cell holds 3, not 1, and the == 1 comparison does not see it. The middle cell of the triple survives and becomes 3; when the code reaches the bottom middle, it sees only two of its three live neighbors — and it is not born. Count a neighbor by its low bit: live += b[ny][nx] & 1.
cards/10/title: A flat grid in a game: edges, padding, Jobs
cards/10/body:
In a flat array, neighbors are index offsets: right i + 1, left i − 1, the adjacent rows i ± w. The trap: for a cell on the right edge, i + 1 is the first cell of the next row. The array will not throw, and the bug will be silent. Check the edge by x, not by the index.

Padding: a (w + 2)×(h + 2) grid with a ring of “walls” around the edge. Inner cells never go out of bounds, the checks disappear, and the neighbor offsets are constants { +1, −1, +W, −W } with width W = w + 2.

Unity: a flat NativeArray<int> goes into an IJobParallelFor over cells, compiled with Burst. For an automaton like Game of Life use two buffers: the job reads the old one and writes the new one, because a parallel job must not write where its neighbors read. Tilemap is slow for logic: read a block via GetTilesBlock into an array, compute on the array, write back with SetTilesBlock.
cards/10/deep:
T[,] in .NET. Multidimensional array access has historically been slower than one-dimensional: the index is computed from each dimension’s lower bound and length, and the JIT is worse at removing the bounds checks. Newer .NET versions narrowed the gap, but on Mono and IL2CPP in Unity the flat array is the most predictable option. Measure with the profiler, not by faith.

Bounds checks. In a loop for (int i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) a[i] the JIT removes the check. For a row of a jagged array, put it in a local, var row = g[y];, and loop to row.Length. For a flat one — Span<int> row = cells.AsSpan(y * w, w) (available in Unity too).

Burst vectorizes simple loops over a NativeArray; branches and calls inside get in the way. In an IJobParallelFor the safety system only lets you touch a writable container within the indices of the current batch — a write to a neighbor is stopped with an error until the restriction is lifted with [NativeDisableParallelForRestriction] (and then the races are your problem). A [ReadOnly] container can be read at any index — hence the scheme “old buffer read-only, new buffer written at your own cell”.

An infinite board is a common follow-up to #289: store only the live cells in a HashSet<(int, int)> and, for the next generation, count neighbors for the live cells and their neighbors — O(live) instead of O(wh). Games split an infinite world into chunks (say 32×32), each a flat array, and do not store empty chunks.

Two bits versus two buffers. Bits halve the memory, but one array is both read for neighbors and written: in a single-threaded loop that is safe, but a parallel job cannot do it — formally it is a race, and the safety system will not let you read other cells of a writable container. Two buffers cost twice the memory, but the old buffer is read-only, and traversal order does not matter.
cards/11/q: A flat w×h grid, cell i = y * w + x. What is true? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: The right neighbor is i + 1, but only if x + 1 < w; otherwise it is a cell of the next row
cards/11/options/1: The neighbor in the next row is i + w
cards/11/options/2: The i + 1 bug on the right edge always ends in IndexOutOfRangeException
cards/11/options/3: With a one-cell padding ring, inner cells are visited without bounds checks
cards/11/options/4: In an IJobParallelFor the automaton can be updated in place: the jobs will agree on an order
cards/11/explain: i + 1 on the right edge is the first cell of the next row: the index is inside the array, there is no exception, the bug is silent (it only throws for the very last cell). The next row is +w. Padding makes every offset of an inner cell safe. Parallel jobs do not coordinate an order: an in-place update creates races — you need two buffers.
cards/12/q: You are solving Game of Life out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: the rules, simultaneous update, in place or not, what lies beyond the edge
cards/12/items/1: Naively: a copy of the grid — O(wh) memory
cards/12/items/2: Idea: bit 0 is the current state, bit 1 the next one
cards/12/items/3: First pass: count neighbors by cell & 1, mark future life with cell |= 2
cards/12/items/5: Walk through three cells in a row: they become a vertical triple
cards/12/items/6: Complexity O(wh) time, O(1) memory; the follow-up is an infinite board
cards/12/explain: The key word is “simultaneously”: it explains why writing immediately breaks the neighbors and why the second bit is needed. Three in a row is the best example: it also catches the == 1 instead of & 1 bug.
cards/13/q: Match each storage option or technique with its property.
cards/13/pairs/0/1: One block, [y, x], sizes via GetLength
cards/13/pairs/1/1: Rows are separate objects, grid[y] is a whole row
cards/13/pairs/2/1: One bounds check, ready for NativeArray and Burst
